title: Can the wave be drawn on a line of another length?
description: The wave is drawn again on a central line of twelve centimetres. The video halves the line, halves again to get the opening of the compass, places the two tips and checks the wave against the line.
teaching_notes: One idea: for any central line, the opening of the compass is the line divided by four. Watch for children who copy the opening of two centimetres from the book's line of eight centimetres.

source: Take a central line of a different length and try to draw the wave on it.
video_script.why: The child repeats the halving method of the solved wave on a line of a new length.
video_script.substitution: A central line of twelve centimetres, with X halfway.
video_script.anchor: The wave along a central line AB of twelve centimetres
video_script.payoff_line: For a line of twelve centimetres, the opening is three centimetres.

final_answer.value: open ended; for a line of length L the opening is L / 4, so for L = 12 cm it is 3 cm
final_answer.spoken: for a line of twelve centimetres the opening is three centimetres, a quarter of the line

never_show: the answer before the last beat
maths_rules: AB = 12 cm; X halfway: AX = 12 / 2 = 6 cm.
Opening = half of AX = 6 / 2 = 3 cm, which is AB / 4 = 12 / 4 = 3 cm.
First tip: 3 cm from A. Second tip: 6 + 3 = 9 cm from A.
Check: 3 + 3 = 6 cm = AX, and 6 + 6 = 12 cm = AB.
video_script.design: One idea: halve the line twice. Uses the method of the solved wave. The line AB stays all video.

beats.on_screen: Answer: for AB = 12 cm, opening 3 cm, a quarter of the line; tips at 3 cm and 9 cm from A
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>For a line of twelve centimetres, the opening is three centimetres.
The opening is always a quarter of the line, whatever its length.
